newsitem.title: GERMANY: Havel urges Germans, Czechs to use historic chance.
newsitem.headline: Havel urges Germans, Czechs to use historic chance.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel urged Germans and Czechs on Thursday to seize a historic chance to set aside resentment left over from World War Two and work together for European integration.

Havel's speech to the German parliament was the latest in a series of steps intended to help overcome the legacy of Hitler's occupation of Czech lands and establish the same untroubled relations which Germany has with other wartime victims.
The playwright and former anti-communist dissident was one of the initiators of a bilateral declaration of reconciliation signed earlier this year after two years of tortuous talks.

"By freeing us all from our fear of the truth, the declaration creates an exceptionally favourable climate to develop our neighbourly co-existence and co-operation on the European stage," he said. "This is a truly historic chance which must not be wasted."

In the declaration, Bonn expresses sorrow for the Nazi occupation, and Prague its regret for the brutal postwar expulsion of 2.5 million ethnic Germans -- issues which have beset relations even after the end of the Cold War.

Havel, one of the first Czech politicians to urge his countrymen not to blame all the ethnic Germans collectively for backing the Nazis, said the declaration could not instantly dispel years of bitterness and misunderstanding.
But he said it would show Europe that both states were determined not to carry historical baggage into every negotiation.

"Just as today's Germany is not in a position to bring back to life the tens of thousands of Czech victims of the Nazis and take us back to the time before 1938 where Czechs, Jews and Germans lived together (in the Czech lands), so today's Czech Republic cannot give the Germans who were expelled their homes back."
Havel received a standing ovation from a packed house both as he walked into the chamber and after he finished his 40-minute speech, delivered in Czech.

Even some of the conservative deputies who act as mentors to the "Sudeten Germans" who were driven out of Czech lands wholesale after the war applauded when Havel said it was easier now to accept the expellees in their old homeland:
"They are welcome not just as guests but as our former fellow citizens who have centuries-old roots in our country and a right to expect us to perceive and honour these ties."
The status of these expellees was one of the many issues on which Bonn and Prague had to agree to differ in order to clinch the declaration.

Bonn wanted Prague to concede that the dispossession and expulsion of the Sudeten Germans, many of whom still hope to get their property back, was illegal. Prague wanted Bonn to reject all property claims and pay compensation to war victims similar to that paid to victims in other countries.

In the event, both sides expressed regret for the excesses committed during and after the war, but neither gave any legal ground which might have opened up the possibility of return of property. They set up a fund to finance joint projects, most of which will aim to help surviving victims of the Nazis.
